webTitle: Morning Mail: The public servants paid more than PM; Kean’s climate broadside; and Heeney’s comeback wish

fields.headline: Morning Mail: The public servants paid more than PM; Kean’s climate broadside; and Heeney’s comeback wish
fields.trailText: Parliamentary question reveals 11 officials earn more than $1m; Swans star wins club’s best and fairest and says he’s raring to return
fields.bodyText: Morning everyone. A question on notice submitted by a Greens senator has produced an insight into the pay of top public servants, with 11 paid more than $1m last year. Climate chief Matt Kean has attacked the approval of a huge new coal project in New South Wales, Isaac Heeney says he “can’t wait” to play for the Swans again despite ongoing police investigations, Australian scientists make a breakthrough about a common infection affecting millions of women, and high school protests in France escalate into “urban violence”. Australia Rugby union | The former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who became the first cystic fibrosis sufferer in the world to play a contact sport professionally, has been diagnosed with motor neurone disease aged 37. Pay day | Nearly a dozen federal public servants were paid more than $1m last year, with one receiving a $1.5m package worth more than double Anthony Albanese’s base salary, according to figures released after a Senate question. Kean observation | Matt Kean, the chair of the Climate Change Authority, has challenged the NSW government’s approval of the largest coal mining development in the state’s history, arguing “climate change isn’t someone else’s problem”. Infection clue | Australian scientists have identified two contributors to recurrent bacterial vaginosis infections, a common sexual health condition that affects about one in four women globally. AI opt-out | Anthropic has urged the Albanese government to consider giving “conditional approval” for AI companies to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model, after conceding it would not secure a blanket copyright exemption. ‘Can’t wait’ | Isaac Heeney says he “can’t wait” to continue his AFL career at the Sydney Swans after the midfielder was crowned the club’s best and fairest player. His comments come after serving a club-imposed suspension for breaching club standards in an incident still being investigated by police. World France flashpoint | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils. ‘Fake’ polling | Donald Trump deflected responsibility for misleading Americans about the length of the Iran war, dismissed low poll ratings as “fake numbers” and refused to rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency before the midterms, in an interview with Time magazine. The White House has again removed CNN as the primary television pool representative covering Trump. Pilot ‘indoctrinated’ | The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an alleged attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has claimed. Bond sell-off | The global bond sell-off intensified overnight, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in frantic trading, underlining the threat to Australia suggested by RBA governor Michele Bullock yesterday. Execution line | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night. Full Story Greens’ David Shoebridge on his plan to beat One Nation and replace Labor Our political editor, Tom McIlroy, speaks to the new Greens leader about taking on One Nation, pushing back on Aukus, and his vision for the party’s future. In-depth As conflict rages in the Middle East, John Duerden reports on how Yemen’s qualification for the Gulf Cup in Saudi Arabia helped rally the war-torn country. “The people support us,” says the coach, Noureddine Ould Ali. “It is a religion in Yemen. Everyone likes football … The Yemeni people are the same as anyone else.” Not the news Today’s leading question for our advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith is one from someone who says their wife is “obsessed with news from the US” and “literally spends all day sitting on the couch, watching videos and reading opinion pieces”. What to do? Sport Football | The Socceroos’ two excellent performances against Brazil show that the national team are developing a new golden generation around youngsters such as Nestory Irankunda, Lucas Herrington and Paul Okon-Engstler, argues Joey Lynch. Cristiano Ronaldo has had a hissy fit but Portugal face Denmark in the Nations League. NRL | The Roosters are favourites but could the Knights crash the grand final party with their wave of unstoppable form? Golf | Phil Mickelson sought treatment earlier this year for “family trauma and addiction”, his representatives confirmed to multiple outlets on Wednesday. Media roundup Trade minister Don Farrell has suggested to the Trump administration a plan for the $4.8tn superannuation sector to invest in America’s lamb industry to head off additional tariffs, the Australian claims. Climate activists have been banned from entering a weapons expo in Perth, WAtoday reports. What’s happening today Sydney | Arraignment at NSW supreme court for four teenagers after the Wakeley church stabbing. Art | Art Gallery of NSW preview of Sidney Nolan exhibition. webTitle: Trump doesn’t rule out declaring state of emergency before midterm elections

fields.headline: Trump doesn’t rule out declaring state of emergency before midterm elections
fields.trailText: President also dismissed low poll ratings as ‘fake numbers’ and deflected responsibility for Iran war in Time interview
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump deflected responsibility for misleading Americans about the length of the Iran war, dismissed low poll ratings as “fake numbers” and refused to rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency before the midterms, in a wide-ranging interview with Time magazine. When confronted with questions about the length of the Iran war, the US president blamed the media for reporting his remarks in which he said the conflict was projected to last “four to five weeks”, in March. “ … I think the press fed it to them,” Trump told Time when asked whether Americans misunderstood him. At the end of March, Trump had told Americans he planned to wind down the Iran war over the next “two to three weeks”. In May, Trump insisted that a peace deal with Iran was nearly finalized. The US president said that he could have ended the Iran conflict whenever but chose to extend it “because I wanted to go further”. For more than seven months, Americans have been grappling with higher everyday costs as a result of Trump’s war with Iran – from gas prices surpassing $4 per gallon to stubborn inflation hovering at 3.4%. Economic concerns, fueled by Trump’s conflict, have angered voters, most of whom say they are unhappy with the president’s handling of the economy and his job overall. Just 26% of adults said they approve of the economy under the Republican president, according to an Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll. Overall, just 31% of people said they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president. But when asked about his low approval rating during his interview with Time, Trump dismissed concerns. “They’re fake numbers,” Trump said. “I would beat anybody running today by 20 points. Your numbers, that you have, are fake. The pollsters are corrupt. They’re almost as corrupt as the writers.” The US president added: “See, I’m doing very well. I think I am. Look, we have the strongest economy.” Despite Trump’s assertion, Americans do not feel the same way. Approximately 74% of Americans told AP/NORC that the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs. Voters’ frustrations with Trump could affect Republican candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, particularly those closely aligned with the US president. Polls show many Democratic candidates making progress with voters, even in historically conservative states such as Texas. Trump brushed aside the likelihood of Democrats winning, telling Time magazine that, so long as he campaigns with candidates, Republicans could perform well. Some Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that Trump will again make allegations of election fraud if Democratic candidates outperform Republicans in the November elections. Trump refused to concede the 2020 presidential election after losing to Joe Biden. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump has claimed US elections are insecure and signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods – such as restricting mail-in ballot voting and requiring ID. He has previously refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement his desired regulations. Other administration leaders, such as the FBI director, Kash Patel, have not ruled out the possibility of deploying federal law enforcement officers to polling locations, which is against the law. When asked whether he would declare a state of emergency before the midterms, Trump told Time magazine: “I don’t rule anything out or in. We’ll see.” Trump further specified that while he’s never invoked the Insurrection Act, a 19th-century law that allows the president to deploy military troops domestically under specific circumstances, he “could use it”. “A lot of people think I should use it sometimes,” Trump said. Among other topics the president discussed with Time magazine, he responded affirmatively when asked whether he regretted appointing supreme court justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “What can I do? I put them in. They voted against me too often. I was very – I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they voted against me often,” Trump said. The supreme court often votes in favor of the Trump administration but it has ruled against the president – such as in the case challenging his sweeping tariffs and his efforts to roll back birthright citizenship.

webTitle: DNC sues Trump administration over last-minute changes to overseas voting form

fields.headline: DNC sues Trump administration over last-minute changes to overseas voting form
fields.trailText: DNC accuses Pentagon of pushing through changes to how voters abroad request absentee ballots ahead of midterms
fields.bodyText: The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday. Until recently, the form, the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), gave overseas voters four options to choose from when describing their geographic location. Voters could say they needed an overseas ballot because they were on active military service, living outside the US with an intent to return, or living outside the US and uncertain about their return. The form also allowed voters to check a box if they were a US citizen who had never lived in the country (38 states and the District of Columbia allow citizens born abroad to vote in at least some elections even if they have never lived in the country). In August, as the deadline to send out overseas ballots approached, the Pentagon – the agency that oversees the form – submitted two emergency requests to modify the form. Among the changes, the Pentagon sought to eliminate the option allowing voters to say they were citizens who never lived in the US. The requests were quickly approved by the office of management and budget (OMB). NPR first reported the changes earlier this week. “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots. They know that Americans, both at home and abroad, are going to reject their destructive agenda, and they are scrambling to disenfranchise as much of the electorate as possible by any means necessary,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. A Pentagon spokesperson said: “The Department is committed to ensuring all Service members, their families, and overseas citizens have seamless access to the tools and resources to successfully exercise their right to vote from anywhere in the world. “To actively protect voting rights and eliminate voter confusion, FVAP.gov is routinely updated to ensure all online tools, federally-prescribed forms, and state-specific guidance remain streamlined, legally compliant, and simple to navigate. This includes updated online guidance on August 31 that clarifies instructions and voter eligibility requirements regarding the Federal Post Card Application and Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot,” the spokesperson said. The changes could confuse and discourage US citizens who have never lived in the country from registering and casting a ballot, experts said. “The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act guarantees US citizens abroad, along with service members and their families, the right to vote, and nothing in it requires a plan to return. Changing the form does not change that right. It changes whether a voter recognizes themselves on it,” said Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the US Vote Foundation, which works on helping overseas Americans vote. “If an overseas voter goes on to the FPCA website, goes to get their Federal Postcard Application to request their ballot, they’re going to see this form and they have to sign it under penalty of perjury,” said a DNC official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to candidly discuss the lawsuit. “They’re going to see that there is no longer the checkbox they’re used to checking. And the other options may not fit them accurately and they may not be able to comfortably or confidently sign that form and request their mail ballot.” In an August letter to the OMB, Sean O’Keefe, the deputy undersecretary of defense for personnel and readiness, said the department had recently become aware of the option on the form for citizens who had never lived in the US. The changes were necessary, he said, because the existing versions “may confuse voters about the information they are required to provide under federal law”. He added that the changes could not go through a normal process because the election was less than 90 days away, and therefore had to be rushed. Lawyers for the DNC said in its lawsuit that justification was pretextual and implausible. The government “has at least 15 years of experience issuing guidance to US citizens born and remaining abroad, reviewing public comments concerning use of the FPCA by these applicants, and modifying the FPCA to best serve these eligible voters”, they wrote. By rushing through the changes, the government violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal law that requires government agencies to carefully weigh the impact of rules changes before implementing them. The OMB also did not follow proper procedure by not allowing for public comment in the federal register. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington DC, asks a judge to declare the government violated the APA and to set aside the government’s changes to the form. There are an estimated 2.2 million US citizens living abroad who are eligible to vote, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (the highest number of eligible citizens are living in Canada and the UK). About 11% of eligible US citizens living abroad voted in 2024. It’s not immediately clear how many US citizens live abroad but have never lived in the country. A 2016 government report estimated there were about 11,590, though lawyers for the DNC believe the number has increased since then. The Pentagon changed the form as the Republican National Committee (RNC) has pushed to prevent US citizens who have never lived in the country from having their votes counted. Republicans have sued in nine states challenging the policy of counting ballots for these types of voters. While one North Carolina court agreed with Republicans, several other courts have rejected their arguments while other lawsuits remain pending. In August, around the time the Trump administration rushed through the change, the RNC put out a statement saying it was “leading the fight to shut down a loophole that allows certain people who have never lived in a state to vote in its elections. As the case heads to the Nebraska supreme court, the RNC is pushing to protect residency requirements and stop the spread of ‘never-resident’ voting nationwide.” “The RNC strongly agrees that every eligible US citizen should be able to vote. The difference is the DNC wants to extend voting rights to people who aren’t eligible. Enforcing citizenship and residency requirements isn’t disenfranchisement – it’s following the law,” Ally Triolo, the RNC’s communications director for election integrity issues, said in a statement. “Regardless of the number of people at issue, as the DNC, we want to defend the rights of Americans to vote – of eligible US citizens to vote at home and abroad,” the DNC official said. “It is simply offensive that the RNC is trying to outright disenfranchise eligible US citizens. And it is offensive that [the Pentagon] would be joining that campaign just before the election.”

webTitle: Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors

fields.headline: Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors
fields.trailText: Installing tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to Pentago defense board raises conflict-of-interest concerns
fields.bodyText: By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, bestowed extraordinary influence on two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. The new project, which Hegseth dubbed “Project Meridian” in an event in Quantico, Virginia, on Wednesday, will be led by Pentagon official Emil Michael, a former Uber executive. As the Guardian has reported, Michael made millions in profits off non-public Musk company AI stock while in federal office – and while guiding the Department of Defense’s artificial intelligence efforts. Along with Luckey and Musk, Project Meridian will also include the Trump loyalist and former speaker of the House Newt Gingrich. Musk was one of the chief financiers of Trump’s 2024 victory, spending over a quarter of a billion dollars in the run-up to the election. Recent campaign records show he is still a major force in the coming midterms. His America Pac spent $3.4m attacking the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, for example. In the hotly contested Texas Senate race, America Pac spent $6.4m to oppose Democrat James Talarico and $1m to support the Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton. Musk’s SpaceX has been a crucial contractor for US space programs since 2018, and in the second Trump administration his company has emerged as key player in Trump’s pet Golden Dome ballistic missile defense project, a phenomenally expensive effort that could cost as much as $1.2tn. Musk dwarfs Luckey in resources and fame, but Luckey has achieved immense celebrity in the defense contracting and world. Initially a young celebrity in the tech world for inventing a virtual reality headset, Luckey later founded Anduril, a defense contracting company that has already won significant federal contracts. Luckey has also become of the most important “bundlers” for Republican candidates on the west coast, as the Guardian reported in August. One of the sources called him the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. Invitations to political fundraisers obtained by the Guardian show Luckey hosted and co-hosted events for candidates from Trump himself to Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, Mehmet Oz, Ted Cruz and others. The most recent event was on 22 August, where he and his wife co-hosted a $50,000-a-head effort to “Keep the Senate”, and listing guests John Thune of South Dakota, Mike Rogers of Michigan, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Jon Husted of Ohio. It is not necessarily a mystery what Musk and Luckey think about warfare’s future. The 34-year-old Palmer, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, UAVs, and space technology, has been already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare. Earlier this year, for example, he said he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through he crust of the earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. He has claimed that his company has “working prototypes of subterranean systems”. “Bringing major industry players into these types of positions at the Pentagon is not something new, but what feels different now is the substantial financial support these two have, and continue to, deliver for the Republican party,” said Brendan Glavin of Open Secrets, a non-partisan group that tracks campaign spending. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

webTitle: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles amid Trump pressure

fields.headline: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles amid Trump pressure
fields.trailText: Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
fields.bodyText: Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban. The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves. Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.” Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday. The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks. Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices. It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US. The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC. John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban. EC commission spokesperson Anna Kaisa Itkonen confirmed that EU member states will hold urgent talks with the commission on Friday to discuss a coordinated response. “The commission … is closely coordinating with EU member states to take stock of the situation and examine appropriate measures to tackle these high prices,” Itkonen added. Discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency. The US energy secretary Chris Wright said he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global fuel ⁠prices by drawing down its emergency diesel inventories. “This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go ⁠into to harvest season and we go into winter heating oil season,” he told Fox ⁠News. “Now’s the time to bring more ‌diesel to the market, and that diesel is available.” Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns. Earlier, a US official told reporters it was “in Europe’s best interest” to ⁠work with the US as it pursues options to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers. The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday. Releasing more stocks would represent a problem for European countries, which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues. “The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added. Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies. A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

webTitle: Lawmakers call for action on ‘plainly illegal’ taxpayer-funded ads to promote Trump

fields.headline: Lawmakers call for action on ‘plainly illegal’ taxpayer-funded ads to promote Trump
fields.trailText: House Democrats say officials may have illegally misused public funds to pay for president’s ‘narcissistic ego trips’
fields.bodyText: The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections. Two congressional Democrats, Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads. Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”. The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government. “President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.” The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable. The lawmakers say the ads may violate four sets of laws, and cited a provision in this year’s spending act that bars funds for “publicity or propaganda”, along with the Anti-Deficiency Act, federal criminal statutes on misusing public money and the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act exempts the president but covers executive branch staff, and the lawmakers argue that employees must have helped produce the ads. Raskin and Whitesides reject the White House’s description of the ads as public service announcements. They say nearly every claim in them is false, and that they are virtually identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ads. In one example, they say an ad credits Trump with reviving manufacturing, though the US has lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in his second term, according to a February report from Congress’s joint economic committee. They also challenge the White House’s argument that the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot, though at an August rally he urged supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot”. A White House spokesperson has called the ads “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. Trump said on Wednesday that he would “gladly pay the money” if the ads were found to be improper. Some Republicans have also raised concerns. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, and the senators Mike Rounds, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis have questioned the use of public money, while the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair, Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said the ads were appropriate. The ads are not the first administration advertising spending to draw scrutiny. Last year the Department of Homeland Security under Kristi Noem spent more than $200m on ads promoting her and Trump’s immigration policies. In March, Noem testified that Trump had approved the campaign (which the president denied to Reuters), and he then removed her from the secretary role, relegating her to special envoy of the “Shield of the Americas”.

webTitle: Trump and his allies credit deportations with record low crime. Experts disagree

fields.headline: Trump and his allies credit deportations with record low crime. Experts disagree
fields.trailText: Administration says increased immigration enforcement led to fewer homicides, but they have been on the decline since Joe Biden’s term
fields.bodyText: Over the last year and a half, the US has seen a historic drop in homicides. Researchers and reporters are still puzzling through the complex set of reasons why - from the easing of pandemic-era stressors and the Biden administration’s investments in community-based violence prevention to policing and other factors. But for the Trump administration, there’s one easy explanation: increased immigration enforcement. As the midterm elections approach, the White House has been doubling down on this message, saying its crackdown against immigrants is why US crime rates are now falling. “We have the most secure border in the world, nobody comes in, unless they’re invited. Unless they have permission,” Trump said during a speech to the UN general assembly last week. “As a result, last year we achieved the largest drop in violent crime ever recorded.” JD Vance, the vice-president, made a similar claim at a rally in Iowa the week prior. “When you get the violent criminals out of your country you see the largest drop in violent crime in the history of the United States of America,” he said. “Murder rates, because we got the bad guys out.” But experts say this simply isn’t true. There’s no data that proves mass deportations or enhanced immigration enforcement leads to lower crime rates, and the research that does exist shows there is no relationship between immigrants – documented or not – and homicide rates in the US, experts say. “It’s a specious claim if you’ve never attempted to verify anything with actual facts and are willing to believe what the administration will tell you,” said Pratheepan Gulasekaram, a law professor at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “If you live in a fact-free world this is the type of nonsensical data you’re willing to imbibe.” In addition, the plummeting homicide rate the US is experiencing now didn’t start during Trump’s second term. It started in 2023, when Biden was president, researchers say. Even though there’s no evidence to back up the Trump administration’s claims, Gulasekaram said xenophobia is one reason why they resonate with many Americans. “There’s an intuitive appeal to that claim if you start with the premise that foreigners are so different from us and are the source of economic and social ills,” he said. “That feeds into that underlying sentiment and it becomes extremely sticky.” Other conservatives are echoing the White House’s unsubstantiated claims by making the same link between immigrants and crime. In a May Instagram video, Erich Pratt, vice-president of Gun Owners of America argued that Americans are “enjoying unprecedented safety”, because of the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. “It didn’t come from new gun restrictions,” he said in an email to the Guardian of the plummeting homicide rates across the US. “It came from a shift in priorities. President Trump implemented measures aimed at deporting violent gang members, ending catch-and-release policies for illegal aliens, and getting repeat offenders off the streets.” A Guardian analysis published in February showed that more than 75% of people who entered deportation proceedings for the first time had no criminal convictions. Only 34 of more than 18,400 people arrested by ICE between 2025 and June this year were convicted of killing someone, according to DHS data. The most common convictions were for illegal re-entry, driving under the influence and a category marked as “other”. It’s unclear how many undocumented migrants are currently in prison for murder convictions or have been convicted for killing someone since Trump took office. State prisons track demographic information such as age, race and type of conviction but, with the exception of Texas, immigration status is not one of them. And by the federal government’s own acknowledgment, there is no comprehensive or centralized data on the citizenship status of people incarcerated in local jails and state prisons, the government accountability office said in a 28 September report. Still, Trump has spent a decade claiming, without evidence, that undocumented migrants pose a safety threat to US citizens. In his 2016 presidential run, he repeatedly talked about the killing of Kate Steinle, a 32-year-old woman who had been killed in San Francisco the year before. The man accused of killing her was undocumented, but he was eventually acquitted. And during his 2024 run, he often spoke of Laken Riley, a nursing student who was killed while she was jogging. Her killer was an undocumented immigrant, and was sentenced to life in prison. Researchers say that stories like these have long been used to push for tougher immigration policies and more deportations. “The argument in their tragic cases is that they should have never been at risk because this person should have never been able to commit these crimes,” said Michael Light, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “But that’s more of a political disagreement than an empirical one.” Leaning on these kinds of anecdotes to determine immigration policy, and then claiming that they have led to public safety can cause misunderstandings of why homicides and other crimes have decreased, Light said. “There’s no question that they’ve increased enforcement and we’ve seen a historic decrease in homicides,” he said. “But the idea that immigration policy is the only thing that’s changed is problematic. And if we misdiagnose what’s actually driving the homicide decline, that’s going to lead to bad public policy.” This week, the Department of Justice announced a new $25m grant program to support people whose loved ones were killed or injured by undocumented migrants and fund law enforcement efforts to prevent future deaths. The Guardian approached the DHS and the White House to request any data or research that can prove a causal relationship between immigration enforcement and the declining homicide rate. Both agencies reiterated their claims that deportations are the reason homicides are down, but did not supply any evidence.

webTitle: Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea? | Arwa Mahdawi

fields.headline: Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea?
fields.trailText: As the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking point
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump seems to spend an unusual amount of time thinking about toilets. Back in 2019, he bizarrely claimed: “People are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times as opposed to once.” He repeated this claim at a Michigan rally the following year. “Ten times, right, 10 times,” Trump complained. “Not me, of course not me, but you,” he added while pointing at an unfortunate audience member. A couple of years later, he was back to the toilet talk: angrily disputing claims by the New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman that he’d once clogged a White House toilet by attempting to dispose of documents in it. I regret to inform you that the president is once again responsible for a national conversation about toilets. In a fitting encapsulation of Trumpism, explosive diarrhea has become a midterm talking point. Food recalls and stomach-churning parasites have been a mainstay of the news this year and Democrats are milking the issue. In August, for example, the Democratic party’s official Twitter/X account highlighted the number of foods that have been recalled in 2026 and demanded that RFK Jr resign from his role as health secretary. Last month (which happened to be Food Safety Month – who knew?), the Rhode Island congressman Gabe Amo argued that Trump’s cuts to the federal workforce had contributed to decreased food safety. Senator Elizabeth Warren similarly accused “slashed food safety agencies” of contributing to the “cyclospora outbreak” and demanded Trump be held accountable in November. To be fair, the number of food recalls during Trump’s second term is not remarkably different than it was under Joe Biden. What is different, however, is the scale of the problem. The US only recently declared the end of the largest ever recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak, which was linked to contaminated lettuce. That resulted in 570 hospitalizations and two ⁠deaths. Also different is the fact that, as Warren noted, the Trump administration seems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe. Ever since 1995, there has been a federal-state partnership called the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) which tracks infections caused by various pathogens, including Cyclospora. Starting on 1 July, however, the CDC downgraded this program so that mandatory surveillance for the 10 state health departments that participate in the program was limited to salmonella and E coli. This downgrading of pathogen surveillance didn’t cause the cyclospora outbreak, but it might have made it harder for health authorities to respond to it. And it’s not just food that the current administration is making less safe: the air we breathe and the water we drink are all getting more dangerous in the name of maximizing corporate profits. On Monday, for example, the Trump administration announced it was relaxing rules that govern how fuel-efficient auto companies have to make their new gasoline-powered cars and light trucks. The rationale given by Sean Duffy, the reality show star turned transportation secretary, is that removing stringent pollution-control requirements will reduce the average costs of new vehicles by $1,300. We’ll see if that actually happens (corporations are not keen on passing on cost savings), but even if it does reduce car prices, it’s going to cost consumers and the environment in other ways. Reduced efficiency will increase fuel spending, for one thing. And the change is poised to create more air pollution and worsen climate change. The Trump administration is also working to roll back regulation of toxic air pollutants. Earlier this year the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed weakening air pollution limits on ethylene oxide (EtO), a known carcinogen that is used to clean medical devices. A Biden-era rule finalized in 2024 required stringent testing for hazardous emissions and required emitters to cut the amount of EtO they were producing. If the EPA is successful in overturning these rules, then tons of the carcinogenic gas will continue to be released into the community. And it’s obviously not people in the vicinity of Mar-a-Lago breathing in the brunt of this poisonous air, is it? It’s people in largely low-income neighborhoods. Then there’s our water supply. A Biden-era rule set drinking-water limits for several Pfas (commonly known as “forever chemicals”). You know what happened next, don’t you? The Trump administration is trying to roll back those limits, arguing that the standards are expensive and legally flawed. They’ve also terminated a regulatory review of Pfas-contaminated sewage sludge fertilizer that is used on farmland. What does that mean? Well, according to comments submitted by the Southern Environmental Law Center to the EPA, “if PFOA levels are 9.4 parts per billion [as witnessed in sludge tested in Maine], then more than 54 children out of 10,000 who eat 1-2 meals of fish per week on crop farms could get cancer later in life from those meals alone.” In short: if you thought the diarrhea-inducing lettuce was bad, then I’m afraid things only look likely to get worse. If Trump isn’t reined in at the midterms, the whole country is going down the toilet. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

webTitle: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump

fields.headline: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump
fields.trailText: US president blames attacks for driving up fuel prices before midterms, though analysts say his Iran war is main cause
fields.bodyText: Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday. Diesel prices in the US have risen to record highs in recent weeks, adding to cost of living pressures that have helped push Trump’s approval ratings to a career low before next month’s crucial midterm elections. Energy analysts, however, have pointed to the war in Iran and wider disruption to global oil markets as the leading drivers of the price increases. Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have nevertheless emerged as an additional headache for Trump, with the attacks also contributing to tighter diesel supplies at a politically sensitive moment for the US president. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations. The Ukrainian president on Thursday also said the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, which has a range of 200km and was developed by the Ukrainian defence firm FirePoint, had been deployed for the first time. Zelenskyy accompanied the statement with footage of a missile launch, but did not disclose when or where the weapon had been used. Speaking at the Valdai discussion club, Vladimir Putin on Thursday acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had cost the country roughly 1% of its GDP. Earlier this week, Russia – traditionally the world’s second-largest diesel exporter – extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, adding further pressure to a global supply crunch. Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies, said it was unlikely Kyiv would stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure as long as Moscow continued its daily attacks on Ukraine. “There is no rationale for Ukraine to continue exercising restraint while it is being bombarded and major urban areas are under constant attack,” he said. “We need to deprive Russia of revenue,” he added. Zelenskyy has been pushing for a US-brokered energy ceasefire with Russia, but Putin has shown little interest in the proposal, instead vowing to intensify strikes on Ukraine. At Valdai, Putin called “absurd” a proposal he said was be discussed, under which Russia would stop striking Ukrainian vessels if Ukraine halted attacks on Russian oil refineries. In wide-ranging comments at the forum, Putin said Moscow was not on the verge of attacking foreign factories producing weapons for Ukraine, but that such facilities were something Russia’s military and intelligence services needed to monitor closely. He also ramped up his nuclear rhetoric, warning that Russia would consider using “all types of weapons” if its exclave of Kaliningrad was attacked, while insisting that Moscow had “no intention of attacking anyone”. Tensions over the exclave have risen this week, with Russia previously sending a letter to Nato warning it would be ready to resort to using nuclear weapons if the western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad. Meanwhile, Russia has continued its deadly missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, targeting energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and other businesses in an apparent effort to cripple the country’s economy and render Kyiv increasingly uninhabitable. A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday morning, but no one was injured because the children were sheltering in the basement, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. A key bridge in the Ukrainian capital was also hit, forcing authorities to suspend metro services and other public transport. Kyiv has experienced near round-the-clock Russian attacks in recent weeks, at times increasingly resembling a frontline city in what many see as the most challenging period for the capital since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Russia’s newer jet-powered drones have proved particularly difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, with success rates significantly lower than for the slower Shahed-type drones. The sustained attacks have revived fears of another winter with prolonged power and heating outages, after similar strikes last year left parts of Ukraine without electricity during temperatures that fell as low as -20C (-4F).

webTitle: White House airs new taxpayer-funded ad praising Trump’s war on Iran

fields.headline: White House airs new taxpayer-funded ad praising Trump’s war on Iran
fields.trailText: New ad features audio from Trump’s declaration of war and Pete Hegseth saying ‘if you kill Americans … we will kill you’
fields.bodyText: The latest in a series of pro-Trump television ads aired using taxpayer funds in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a one-minute spot that celebrates Donald Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. The ad aired during a commercial break on Fox News on Wednesday night, according video posted online by MeidasTouch, a leftwing outlet. A copy of the new ad posted on social media by Medium Buying, a company that purchases airtime for Republican candidates, features audio taken from the president’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations in Iran. “This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States armed forces,” Trump can be heard saying over images of combat, some of which appear to be dramatizations or computer-generated. A cover version of John Lee Hooker’s Boom Boom provides the soundtrack. The audio then switches to comments made by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, in a briefing on the third day of the war. “He reminded the world, as he has time and time again, being an American means something unbreakable,” Hegseth says over slow-motion images of Trump walking down a corridor. “If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth says. “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it. Their war on Americans has become our retribution against their ayatollah.” As the words “Paid for by the US Government” appear at the bottom of the screen, the ad’s audio switches back to Trump’s call for regime change in Iran in his announcement of the war in February. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump can be heard saying, against a backdrop of dramatic music and images of Iranian Americans in New York celebrating the US strikes on 1 March. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take.” The images of Iranian Americans demonstrating in support of Trump’s war in New York City, marching down 42nd Street and holding signs that read “Thank you President Trump”, were all previously included in a White House video posted on YouTube on 4 March. The focus of the ad on speeches and images of celebration that all came in the first three days of the war, when it looked like Iran’s government could collapse, raises questions about why the administration is releasing it as the war enters its seventh month and continues to alienate many of Trump’s supporters.

webTitle: ‘Page one of repressive playbook’: critics warn of Trump’s conspiratorial attacks

fields.headline: ‘Page one of repressive playbook’: critics warn of Trump’s conspiratorial attacks
fields.trailText: President’s outlandish and extensive conspiracy theories endanger US freedoms, health and science, experts say
fields.bodyText: Since the start of his second presidency, Donald Trump has often launched outlandish conspiratorial attacks on critics and foes that mock them and label their views as hoaxes, prompting scholars and legal experts to say Trump’s attacks endanger US freedoms, public health and science. Trump’s extensive use of conspiracy theories is the hallmark of an authoritarian leader that has weakened trust in the coming midterm elections, dangerously ignored scientific evidence, and often pushed for prosecutions of his political enemies in ways that seriously erode civil liberties, say critics. Trump’s conspiratorial and authoritarian-style tactics are palpable say critics, in his false claim that the US faces a “crisis of election security” to bolster his radical push for new curbs on voting rights, and his labeling of climate change as a “hoax” despite extensive scientific evidence that it’s a reality. To some scholars, Trump-backed conspiratorial claims have had a damaging impact on all levels of US society and democracy and are emblematic of how authoritarian leaders use conspiracies to justify repression. Steven Levitsky, the Harvard professor of government and the co-author of How Democracies Die, said: “Conspiracies are page one of the repressive playbook,” noting that Mao, Stalin, Putin and other authoritarian leaders have historically launched attacks on enemies by floating conspiracies. “They’re almost always used to justify repression,” Levitsky added noting that authoritarian leaders can simply allege conspiracies without providing any or only minimal “evidence”. In a notable twist, Trump charged in mid-September that some AI leaders and experts were engaging in a big “conspiracy” and perpetrating a “HOAX”, by urging strong safeguards to protect against potential extinction-level threats to humanity from this powerful new technology. Similarly, Trump without evidence disparaged critics of datacenters as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor”, and asserted he was the best “guardrail” to protect society from threats that unregulated AI pose. Scholars and former federal officials say that Trump’s tarring foes in conspiratorial attacks endangers democracy and recall the tactics of the infamous rightwing lawyer Roy Cohn, a key promoter of the “red scare” in the 1950s who Trump had close ties with in the 1980s during his early New York real estate career. “Trump, mentored by Roy Cohn, learned that baseless allegations about shady forces working against him could serve to mobilize and lead the public to see him as a victim rather than a wrongdoer,” said the Princeton historian Julian Zelizer. “Whenever faced with criticism, such as from the media or about his AI policies, his instinct is to throw out charges of a vast conspiracy that is out to get him.” Zelizer stressed: “Trump’s frequent use of conspiracies to attack critics has a damaging impact on all levels of society and democracy, from weakening confidence in elections to hurting our ability to deal with serious problems involving the AI industry.” Trump’s penchant to paint critics in conspiratorial tones as dangerous enemies was palpable in his attacks last week on three news outlets – CNN, Politico and MS Now – barring them from White House access which prompted them to jointly file a lawsuit on 21 September challenging his moves on First Amendment and due process grounds. In a Truth Social post on 21 September, Trump boasted that the White House “is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” A federal judge in DC ruled on 23 September that the administration should immediately return the press passes to the three outlets and its punitive action against them was probably unconstitutional. Former federal prosecutor Ty Cobb who was a special counsel in the White House during Trump’s first term, warned that “Trump denies, denigrates and demeans his foes by painting them as part of a conspiracy … He resorts to abject fabrications in response to any criticism or resistance.” This year Trump and his justice department have devoted sizable resources to bolster his conspiratorial claims that his 2020 loss to Joe Biden was due to fraud, and that the current voting system is riddled with fraud, notwithstanding overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Trump has repeatedly pushed bogus claims laced with conspiracies as he did in a nationally televised speech on 16 July, when he urged tough new measures to curb voting by mail and investigate non-citizen voting ostensibly to make elections more secure. In the TV speech, Trump made the factually inaccurate claim that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically negligible, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s obsession with painting non-citizen voting as a crisis is badly undercut by data from the conservative Heritage Foundation that cites just 100 cases over a 25-year period. Critics see these moves by Trump to raise bogus fears about election safety and dark forces bent on voter fraud as a tool to “undermine public confidence” in the elections. “It seems that the Trump administration is grooming the electorate to believe that the fall election will abound with fraud,” said Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney who teaches law at the University of Michigan. “It is difficult to know if this effort is a pretext for seizing voting equipment, a strategy to intimidate some likely Democratic voters from showing up at the polls, or a campaign to undermine public confidence in the outcome, but all of it is harmful to democracy.” On another front, Trump’s justice department has struggled for almost a year to find evidence to bring charges in an investigation looking at a “grand conspiracy” against Trump involving the so called “deep state” going back to President Barack Obama and inquiries into Russia’s efforts to influence the 2016 election. The investigation, which Trump has cheered on, has issued subpoenas to several former national security and law enforcement officials including ex-CIA director John Brennan and ex-FBI director James Comey. This sprawling inquiry has tapped some key Trump-allied election denialists for top posts. Notably, Trump recruited 81-year-old Joe diGenova, a former prosecutor who led the effort until he abruptly announced his departure on 10 September, and ex-White House lawyer Kurt Olsen. Both lawyers had worked to discredit the 2020 election results and Joe Biden’s win. The sudden move by diGenova to resign – after only five months on the job – raised questions about its direction and credibility. DiGenova’s departure followed that of another top prosecutor who was heading the investigation; Maria Medetis Long, a veteran national security prosecutor, resigned in April after reportedly voicing concerns about its direction. “The so-called Grand Conspiracy investigation turns prosecutorial practice on its head,” said ex-justice department inspector general Michael Bromwich who has represented ex-FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe in the inquiry. “It starts with designated targets, the president’s perceived enemies, and then searches for facts and bends the law to support the theory. Joe diGenova found that it was easier to be an outside propagandist cheering the theory from the sidelines than have the responsibility to build such a case with actual facts.” In other energy and environmental matters, Trump and his top officials have deployed bogus conspiracies and specious information to counter growing evidence of the risks posed by climate change from rising temperatures to dangerous storms worldwide. The Trump administration has moved hard to kill energy and environmental regulations aimed at fighting climate change, and simultaneously have promoted greater usage of coal, which Trump has lauded erroneously as “clean and beautiful”, and other fossil fuels that worsen climate change. Late last year, Trump energy officials issued emergency orders to keep open five ageing coal plants in Michigan and four other states that were scheduled to shut down, spurring some states to challenge the costly moves. In mid-September, a federal judge ruled that the energy department had exceeded its authority by ordering the Michigan plant to stay open past its retirement. Further, after years of conspiratorial attacks on wind energy by Trump, his administration in December announced it was pausing leases on five offshore wind projects on the east coast in a big blow to the industry. The five windfarms were slated to power over 2.5m homes and create 10,000 jobs. A federal judge in February issued a preliminary injunction allowing one of the five to stay open. “Trump’s decisions make no sense from either the perspective of environmental protection or the cost of energy,” Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard University science historian and professor of earth and planetary sciences, told the Guardian earlier this year. Oreskes added that “by blocking wind projects that [were] just about ready to go on line, and reviving dangerous and uneconomic coal-powered plants, this administration is raising both the direct costs of energy for the American people, and the indirect costs we suffer through polluted air and climate damage.” Significantly, the Trump administration in February revoked a major scientific finding that climate change endangers public health, an idea that Trump has derided as “a scam”, despite numerous scientific studies saying it’s a well quantifiable harm. Dr Howard Frumkin, a professor emeritus of public health at the University of Washington told PBS: “It boggles the mind that the administration is rescinding the endangerment finding; it’s akin to insisting that the world is flat or denying that gravity is a thing.” In healthcare too, Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services (HHS) who has a long history of making factually erroneous claims about vaccine safety, have indulged in flawed and conspiratorial claims about vaccines. Trump declared flatly in August that the combined MMR vaccine for children could be “quite lethal”, but failed to offer scientific evidence to back his claim. Trump too has advocated breaking up longstanding immunizations into three separate shots that currently are not available in the United States. Even as the death toll from the worst outbreak of measles in decades rises, Kennedy on 16 September starred at a Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he spearheaded for almost two decades. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy told the gathering in an almost 90-minute talk. “You have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time.” According to recent polls about one-quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines in the wake of multi-year campaigns against immunizations by groups that once were fringe figures. From a historical perspective, Zelizer noted that conspiracy theories in American politics have a long history, but that before Trump “the role of presidents and other high-level elected officials had been to push back against this part of politics, rather than to amplify these ideas.”

webTitle: Trump the environmentalist? How his Iran war exposed the fragility of dirty energy

fields.headline: Trump the environmentalist? How his Iran war exposed the fragility of dirty energy
fields.trailText: Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security
fields.bodyText: Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist. Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran. “He’s woken the world up to how vulnerable we are to petro-dictatorships, how vulnerable we are to disruptions in the Middle East,” Newsom told the Guardian during Climate Week in New York. “This war has completely gutted any sort of romantic notions of energy security and it’s compelled folks to think differently. It’s accelerating investments and clean energy and renewables.” If Trump has been an accidental environmentalist, it’s been in the international sphere. The strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports usually flow, is now starting to open up but has been routinely snarled since the Iran war began in February, causing the cost of these fossil fuels to soar around the world. Countries reacted by scrambling to cut their oil and gas use while turning to cleaner forms of energy such as solar and wind (although there’s also been a small rise in coal, the dirtiest of fossil fuels). The overall consequence has been a positive one for our shared climate, with global fossil fuel emissions set to drop by 0.5% this year due to the crisis, Carbon Brief has estimated. The peak in oil consumption may have been sped up enough to arrive this year, rather than the previous estimate of 2029, according to the International Energy Agency. By launching the war, Trump is set to achieve something only dreamed about by climate advocates and not seen outside global economic crashes or the Covid pandemic – an annual reduction in the emissions that are overheating our planet. The president’s imposition of tariffs and importation of foreign ground beef, meanwhile, may also end up hurting the US cattle industry, another major source of greenhouse gas emissions. “It’s a curious thing to say, but I believe it,” Newsom, a potential contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said of Trump as a sort of unintentional biophile. “This moment will mark how we can’t go back to our original form.” Yet the idea of Trump as an environmentalist, even an accidental one, can still appear faintly absurd. His administration has eviscerated pollution limits on cars, trucks and power plants, funnelled taxpayer cash and favors to the fossil fuel industry and set about unilaterally cancelling renewable energy projects. Trump, who has never by available evidence ever set a Florsheimed foot in any of the US’s national parks, has called environmentalists “terrorists”, the climate crisis “a hoax” and has slashed conservation rules to the extent you can now kill a protected species as long as it wasn’t provably intentional. Perhaps tellingly, when asked during the 2024 election campaign about his environmental credentials, Trump cited his Florida golf course getting awards for “the way I built it, for the water, the way I use the water, the sand, the mixing of the sand and the water”. Critics say this record overshadows any embrace of clean energy by other countries spooked by an oil price that has hovered about $100 a barrel for months but should, at some point in the interminable Iran conflict, drop well below this. The impetus for quitting fossil fuels could wither when it does so. “Trump’s illegal attack on Iran may hasten clean energy in some countries, but he has gutted green tech in the United States and set us back decades,” said Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University who said Newsom was guilty of “tunnel vision” in his framing of Trump. “The notion that he is an accidental environmentalist is wishful thinking.” The conflict may have rocked the oil and gas industry but it has also enriched it, netting eight of the largest companies more than $90bn in just the first three months of the war, with even pro-oil Trump complaining that the major fossil fuel firms are “making too much money”. There is little sign big oil fears a looming obsolescence when this bonanza ends. Last month, Exxon forecast that while the world will reduce its emissions, it will still use 105m barrels of oil a day in 2050, up from 100m barrels last year. Two-thirds of the global energy mix will stubbornly remain composed of oil, gas and coal at the midpoint of the century, the oil company estimated. “All of the oil that is produced will be burned – if they produce more, more will be used,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama. “The people who predict that there will be a reduction in the emission of greenhouse gases are simply lying or blind.” The only hope is that the world “can cap consumption and production at levels similar to the ones we have right now”, Navarro added, citing the enormous energy demand of artificial intelligence datacenters, which are largely being run on gas-fired power. However, climate advocates maintain the Iran conflict will accelerate trends that are already swinging behind clean energy. Investment in renewables globally is now double that of fossil fuels, almost all new power being added to grids comes from clean sources and last year one in four cars sold was electric. Unlike previous oil shocks, the world now has a viable alternative to fossil fuels, even if it’s unclear how lasting an impact Trump’s military and trade actions will have in pushing countries towards them. “There is one thing that all these events are making clear,” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission said in April. “We are paying a very high price for our over-dependency on fossil fuels.” Countries from the UK to India to Thailand have sought to speed up the transition to renewables as the price of fossil fuel dependency has spiraled, saving billions. Electric vehicle sales have surged, although not in the US. Trump has urged other countries to reject the “scam” of clean energy but the market is increasingly favoring cheap wind, solar and batteries that have plummeted in cost in recent years, including in the US. “Demand has massively spiked for solar and for battery storage,” said Sonia Dunlop, chief executive of the Global Solar Council. “We’re seeing that all over the world – the Philippines, across Europe, across south-east Asia, Australia and beyond.” “This Iran crisis, which was, in effect, started by President Trump, has led to a massive surge in demand for our technology … but actually it’s just building on a trend that was already there,” she added. Political and business leaders can mull the fact that the wind does not funnel through the strait of Hormuz and the sun doesn’t only shine on a foreign autocrat’s lands. The Iran war may not prove a fatal blow to fossil fuels, but it has starkly highlighted their inherent volatility. The case for renewables has become obvious at a grassroots level in developing countries, too, where rooftops increasingly glitter with cheap Chinese-made solar panels that are helping negate soaring power bills. “The price of solar has come down so quickly that there are now 100,000 solar panels installed every day in Africa,” Al Gore, the former US vice-president, said last week. “In parts of Pakistan, a common bride’s dowry is now three panels and an inverter, instead of 10 or 12 goats. It’s beginning to kick into gear.” This momentum won’t stop once the conflict around the Persian Gulf ends, Dunlop insisted. “I don’t think the world is just going to go back to business-as-usual demand of fossil fuels once this crisis ends,” she said. “Once someone decides to step off the fossil fuel rollercoaster, they’re off it.” So does all this, then, make Trump an environmentalist? “I wouldn’t say that,” Dunlop demurred. “He certainly has his own ideas.”

webTitle: Americans are paying millions for a batch of pro-Trump ads | Margaret Sullivan

fields.headline: Americans are paying millions for a batch of pro-Trump ads
fields.trailText: The spots, including a recycled campaign ad, are funded by taxpayers and present the president as a hero
fields.bodyText: The US government is spending millions of taxpayer dollars to get a blatantly partisan message in front of voters as the midterm elections loom. And while these TV ads aren’t explicitly campaign ads, they might as well be. They feature Donald Trump as a hero. They try to scare people into thinking that the US could become a communist country. They take shots at the news media and at vaguely described political enemies. Two Democratic senators, Patty Murray and Chris Murphy, on Tuesday aptly called them “a shockingly corrupt use of taxpayer dollars”. Their funding, through the Department of Homeland Security, may be illegal, according to experts, and is certainly unethical. They lack any hint of the public service message that the White House claims. In fact, they closely fit the defining characteristics of propaganda, as described by the government accounting office, including “self-aggrandizement” or “puffery”. But the agencies or institutions that could do something about them, including the supposedly independent FCC, are eager to do the president’s bidding. Brendan Carr, the FCC chair, is a proud Trump toady, with his thumb on the scale for every Trump project. Carr has shrugged off questions about the ads. They don’t raise any red flags for him; they are quite normal, and nothing that his agency intends to investigate. And with both houses of Congress held by Republican majorities, this startling use of taxpayer money will probably go unpunished – at least for now. “The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress,” said Donald Sherman, who heads Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (Crew) in Washington. However, as he told CNN, Congress “has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable”. Some Republican members of Congress have questioned the ads, but there’s no groundswell of bipartisan outrage so far. The Trump administration is responding to the criticism with its usual defiance, even planning to double down in the next few weeks. “This is just the beginning,” one administration official told Axios. The argument that these are not political ads is contradicted by an undeniable reality: one of them is a straight-up rerun of a Trump campaign commercial from before the 2024 presidential election. It differs, though, with the addition of an Orwellian coda, “paid for by the US government”. With its weirdly menacing tone, it shows black-and-white images of Trump walking as he promises to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and pledges to “rout out the fake news media”. Another ad shows images of Trump at public events with a voiceover insisting that “America will never be a communist country,” while the song Love Me plays in the background. (The R&B artist JMSN has said he didn’t authorize this use of his song and has made a cease-and-desist demand.) Another ad, reported Robert Tait of the Guardian, shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump bragging: “The United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.” The White House described that “love me” ad as “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. And, in a statement, it termed the various ads as “public service announcements”. They are playing to a big-tent crowd that Trump apparently thinks (or hopes) is persuadable. They’ve aired everywhere from pro-football games to Saturday Night Live. The Wall Street Journal reported that the ads, by last weekend, had aired more than 90 times across various networks – and political leanings – including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now and CBS. As corrupt as they appear to be, the ads do make a twisted kind of Trumpian sense. They are probably illegal and have garnered plenty of legitimate criticism. But what’s missing is accountability with actual teeth. As usual, he’s getting away with it. But the midterm elections could change that. With Trump’s approval ratings low and voters unhappy with misguided Iran war and soaring costs, Democrats could seize a majority in one or both houses of Congress. That might mean some restraints on Trump’s never-ending cascade of malfeasance. It’s no wonder he’s pulling out all the stops to make that nightmare go away. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture
