fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: The latest in a series of pro-Trump ads the Trump administration is using taxpayer funds to air on television in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a 1-minute spot that celebrates his decision to go to war with Iran. Pete Hegseth announced that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, with Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House. An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released Wednesday. The latest in a series of pro-Trump ads the Trump administration is using taxpayer funds to air on television in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a 1-minute spot that celebrates his decision to go to war with Iran. The ad aired during a commercial break on Fox News Wednesday night, according video posted online by MeidasTouch, a leftwing outlet. A copy of the new ad posted on social media by Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, shows that it features audio taken from Donald Trump’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations in Iran. “This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump can be heard saying over images of combat, some of which appear to be dramatizations or computer-generated. A cover version of John Lee Hooker’s Boom Boom provides the soundtrack. The audio then switches to comments made by Pete Hegseth the US defense secretary, in a briefing on the third day of the war. “He reminded the world, as he has time and time again, being an American means something unbreakable,” Hegseth says over slow-motion images of Trump walking down a corridor. “If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth says . “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it. Their war on Americans has become our retribution against their ayatollah”. As the words “Paid for by the U.S. Government” appear at the bottom of the screen, the ad’s audio switches back to Trump’s call for regime change in Iran in his announcement of the war in February. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump can be heard saying, over images of Iranian Americans in New York celebrating the US strikes on 1 March. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take.” The images of Iranian Americans demonstrating in support of Trump’s war in New York City, marching down 42nd Street and holding signs that read “Thank you president Trump”, were all previously included in a White House video posted on YouTube on 4 March. The focus of the ad on speeches and images of celebration that all came in the first three days of the war, when it looked like Iran’s government could collapse, makes its release now, as the war enters its seven month and continues to alienate Trump’s supporters, baffling. A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit against Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, over his refusal to hand over unredacted, sensitive voter information to the Department of Justice. The justice department had demanded that the state’s senior election official email a copy of Georgia’s statewide voter registration list, including each voter’s driver’s license number, social security number and date of birth, arguing that the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law, entitled it to this information. The US district court judge, Victoria Marie Calvert, ruled that the federal law does not require states to disclose sensitive voter data to the federal government, and does not take precedence over Georgia’s state law protecting the privacy of information provided to the state by registered voters. Raffensperger was the Georgia state official Donald Trump called on 2 January 2021, in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election, asking him to “find 11,780 votes” for Joe Biden that could be tossed out as fraudulent, which would have allowed Trump to reverse his loss and win the state by one vote. In keeping with his near-constant use of his office for thinly disguised campaign events, Donald Trump had Alaska’s Republican senator Dan Sullivan by his side in the Oval Office on Wednesday when he announced that South Korea plans to spend $54bn to build a liquefied natural gas pipeline in Alaska. Sullivan is facing a strong challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola to retain his Senate seat in the November midterm elections. Unfortunately for Sullivan, the president wrongly suggested that an issue that is infuriating voters in his home state, the high price of gasoline and diesel, would be solved by the pipeline, which will transport an entirely different kind of petroleum, natural gas, when it is completed in three years. The Alaska LNG project includes an 807-mile (1,299km) pipeline to carry natural gas from the North Slope to a liquefaction facility on Alaska’s southern coast, allowing the fuel to be shipped to Asian markets. Asked by a reporter about whether there has been any discussion of building another oil pipeline in Alaska, given the high cost of gasoline for consumers, Trump appeared to confuse the liquefied natural gas, known as LNG, with gasoline, which is made from oil. “Well, this is going to bring those prices down. One of the reasons, Alaska prices are going to come way down,” Trump said of a project that has nothing to do with gasoline used to fuel cars. After Trump was informed that the the LNG pipeline is going to take three years to complete, which would lower the cost of LNG in Alaska, but have no impact at all on the cost of another petroleum product, gasoline, Trump turned back to reporters and said: “Gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble.” Trump also said that the Korean investment was part of a $200bn package of projects that would also include a 6-gigawatt ⁠power generation facility in Texas, another state where his party is in danger of losing a Senate seat. The announced investment follows pledges South Korea made in 2025 to invest up to $350bn in the US as part of a trade deal in exchange for lower US tariffs on South Korean cars, auto parts and other products. Without providing those details, Trump credited his tariffs for making the announcement possible, saying “our trade agreement with South Korea, they have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars.” “For doing that, I reduced their tariffs to 15%. But they paid to get them reduced,” Trump said. “And, part of that money is going into this project.” Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House. A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations. The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year. Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday that he had spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, about the security incident on a FlyDubai commercial flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel on Wednesday. “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job,” Trump said, before giving a dramatic account of the intervention of a passenger who subdued the pilot who reportedly stabbed his co-pilot. Although witnesses on the flight said that an off-duty pilot then entered the cockpit, pulled the aircraft up and landed in Saudi Arabia, Trump told reporters that “an Israeli plumber” first subdued the attacker, “and this plumber, having never flown a plane, he took the stick, lifted it up, and leveled out the plane before it crashed. Now this is the story that I heard. I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story I got from Bibi.” Before we move on from Pete Hegseth’s lengthy address today, it is worth noting that the Pentagon’s in-house “rapid response” social media account, which is dedicated to battling with the media in the style of a political campaign’s opposition research unit, made a point of highlighting the defense secretary’s scathing criticism of the US press corps. The Pentagon account shared video and a partial transcript of Hegseth addressing reporters he called “the anti-American losers in our media” in prepared remarks that sounded more like a script written by one of Hegseth’s former Fox News producers than a speech by a US cabinet official. Hegseth went on to say: “The information space is a battle space. Yet our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable. Our media’s shameful lust for political retribution blinds them to the consequences of reckless, so-called ‘reporting’. So-called journalists – juiced up on Trump derangement syndrome – think they’re fighting against our president, but they’re really undermining you – our warfighters.” “Bottom line: too many of them hate the president more than they love the country. You see, it’s your movement and bases that they reveal to the enemy,” Hegseth told the troops before him. “And ultimately, it’s your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munitions stockpiles. “All for a banner that will scroll on TV for 30 seconds,” the former Fox weekend host said. “And I know a little bit about banners scrolling on TV for 30 seconds.” Pete Hegseth officially announced 20% cuts to generals and admirals “across the board” in the US military. The defense secretary added that the generals “who clung to the woke department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”. Hegseth appeared to downplay the ongoing mental health crisis in parts of the US military, particularly after eight navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment. Nonetheless, the defense secretary slammed the media, and insisted that there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”. It’s worth noting that Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, confirmed the suicide attempts in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand earlier this month. Throughout his address, Hegseth boasted touted his anti-diversity policies. He insisted that the Pentagon was “no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.” He also announced a new project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with department to study the “future of warfare”. “Their work will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes,” Hegseth said, noting the project’s findings would be completed and submitted within 120 days, culminating in a full public rollout. Meanwhile on Capitol Hill, Senate Democrats blocked legislation that would allow states and utilities to consider standards to ensure tech companies foot the bill for the additional energy costs associated with power-intensive datacenters throughout the US. In a 57-43 vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, four Democrats – Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – all broke with their party in support of the bill. However, the legislation failed to achieve the 60 votes needed to advance out of the Republican-controlled upper chamber. More here Earlier, Democrats in the Senate also blocked legislation that would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and their dependent children from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The Stop Insider Trading Act failed along party lines, in a 53-47 vote, failing to clear the 60-vote threshold. Despite widespread support for stopping members of Congress from trading stocks, many Democrats argued the bill didn’t go far enough to actually solve the issue. They also took issue with the fact that the House-passed bill also included a provision which would require photo identification when casting a ballot. More here Hegseth’s ‘State of the Force’ address also includes an announcement about partnering with a new group of higher education institutions. The defense secretary took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges – which the Trump administration has targeted routinely – as “DEI worshipping woke factories”. Hegseth said the department would now partner with other institutions– some of which are known for conservative values, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College. Other schools joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University. It’s worth remembering that Hegseth attended and graduated from Princeton and Harvard – both Ivy League universities. The defense secretary announced a new Pentagon project that will see Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with department to study the “future of warfare”. “Their work will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes,” Pete Hegseth said, noting the project’s findings would be completed and submitted within 120 days, culminating in a full public rollout. If Palmer Lucky’s name sounds familiar to you, that might be because the Guardian has reported extensively about how his company, Anduril Industries, a major military contractor, has received billions in government contracts over the last year. The first of six announcements the defense secretary made today was the development of a top-level joint military organization, led by four-star generals, to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities. “The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,” Hegseth said. “The autonomous robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades.” Per my last post, Hegseth went on to boast about the retention rates in the US military, claiming they are at “record rates” – including “80% of the force on the USS Abraham Lincoln on their historic mission”. Hegseth appeared to downplay the ongoing mental health crisis in parts of the US military, particularly after eight navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment. Nonetheless, the defense secretary disparaged the media, again, and insisted that there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”. It’s worth noting that Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, confirmed the suicide attempts in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand earlier this month. The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war. As we noted earlier, Pete Hegseth officially announced 20% cuts to generals and admirals “across the board” in the US military. The defense secretary added that the generals “who clung to the woke department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”. As has become customary, Hegseth disparaged the press during his address. “As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment,” he said. “You can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it.” The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, is providing an update on the US military at his second “State of the Force” address, in Quantico, Virginia, one year after he berated “fat troops” and condemned the military’s “woke” policies. Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, Hegseth began his announcements by again boasting about his anti-diversity policies. “The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline, and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues, and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.” The defense secretary added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth said. An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released Wednesday. For over a year, Donald Trump has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair Jerome Powell around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal probe that was dropped in April. The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation. “At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said. Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018m by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027. The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be nonpartisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail. Trump latched onto the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features like a VIP dining room and a garden terrace. In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s. Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures. “It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.” The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said. During his White House event today, Trump spoke to his need for Republicans to secure the Hispanic and Latino vote in the upcoming midterms. “I loved you right from the beginning. I loved you for many years before I ever decided to do this political thing,” the president said. “You also know when I build a wall, I’m building a wall to keep bad people out. And you want, and you want those bad people kept out more than anybody.” This appeal comes after Trump won a record number of Hispanic votes for a Republican president in the 2024 election, but there is concern that the community is now fractured in its support for GOP candidates because of the administration’s immigration crackdown and the cost of living. More than 65% said they are unhappy with the president’s job performance, and 78% said they would prefer to see the Democratic party in control of Congress, according to a recent poll from the New York Times/Siena University. The president falsely claimed that “more oil has come out” of the strait of Hormuz in the past three days than at “any time in history”. While the transport of oil has rebounded in recent weeks, climbing close to prewar levels according to analysts, it has not exceeded that. The increase in flow through the vital waterway is encouraging, according to those tracking the movement, but it hasn’t yet been reflected in the price. The international benchmark for crude oil still sits just below $100 per barrel. Trump also welcomed the Pentagon’s news today that the US has finally completed its withdrawal from Iraq. “This day is a victory for the United States. It’s a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over Isis, which has been completely decimated,” the president said. “I decimated them and took them out in my first administration. So I don’t know what took them so long to be making the announcement that I’m making today.” Speaking at the White House today to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month, Donald Trump told those attending that they would be among the first to see and walk around the new ballroom when he opens the East Room doors after the event. In a 57-43 vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, four Democrats – Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – all broke with their party in support of the bill. However, the legislation failed to achieve the 60 votes needed to advance out of the Republican-controlled upper chamber. Earlier this month, the bill received overwhelming support in the House. However, many Senate Democrats say the bill is “toothless” and doesn’t do enough to actually curb costs for consumers. Datacenter construction and electricity consumption have grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has come increasing anxiety among voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills. Democrats in the Senate blocked legislation that would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and their dependent children from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The House-passed bill would also require that lawmakers disclose that they intend to sell any stocks at least seven days (and up to two weeks) in advance, to curb the ability to profit from insider information. The Stop Insider Trading Act failed along party lines, in a 53-47 vote, failing to clear the 60-vote threshold. Despite widespread support for stopping members of Congress from trading stocks, many Democrats argued the bill doesn’t go far enough to actually solve the issue. “They can’t be serious. The Republican bill is a permission slip for corruption, not a stock-trading ban. This bill has no reform, no accountability, no substance,” said Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader. “Republicans want to explicitly allow members to continue trading stocks in privately held companies, including in companies the members oversee.” Democrats also took issue with the fact that the House-passed bill also included a provision which would require photo identification when casting a ballot. Pete Ricketts, a Republican senator from Nebraska who introduced the legislation in the upper chamber, and who is facing a tough re-election battle in the upcoming midterms, said it was “discouraging” to see his bill fail. The Pentagon announced on Wednesday that it has formally completed its withdrawal of US troops from Iraq, two years after the withdrawal was agreed to and 12 years since the US mission to fight the Islamic State started. After the announcement, Iran and its allies celebrated the departure as a victory, while Iraqi security experts worry that the withdrawal could give the Islamic State and others a chance to recover. “Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq,” the Pentagon said in a statement, adding that the departure of its forces “marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq”. The Pentagon noted it will continue to provide training and intelligence support to Iraq “to ensure ISIS can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory”. The US invaded Iraq in 2003 to oust its dictator, Saddam Hussein, who ruled the country for nearly 24 years. The invasion would lead to hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths, civil war and sectarian violence in Iraq, as well as the rise of the Islamic State militant group. In 2011, Barack Obama declared an end to the Iraq war and announced that all US troops would be withdrawn from the country by year’s end. At that moment, the US military presence in Iraq stood at under 40,000, and 4,400 US military members had been killed. But in 2014, Obama sent troops back to Iraq after Islamic State militants seized large swaths of territory, including Mosul. Then, a coalition of more than 80 countries led by the US was formed to fight Islamic State, which subjugated millions during a cruel war before losing its hold in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019. Finally, in 2024, during Joe Biden’s presidency, the US and Iraq agreed to wind down the US-led coalition operations. The justice department has also announced federal indictments against 10 foreign nationals accused of illegally registering and voting in Minnesota elections. Todd Blanche said a federal grand jury had returned indictments alleging nine counts of illegal voting by an alien and nine counts of falsely claiming US citizenship to register to vote. Charges include illegally voting in the general elections of 2022 and 2024, as well as the state’s primary election in August this year, the attorney general said. “Voter fraud erodes the public’s trust in our electoral system,” Blanche said, adding that a way to restore that trust “is by working to make sure that the only people voting in an election in the United States are American citizens who are eligible to vote”. Since Trump returned to office, according to Blanche, the DoJ has charged more than 90 people with voter-related fraud offenses, including 50 non-citizens in the last five weeks. There are hundreds of investigations going on across the country, he added. In the context of Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, his administration has made a big push to investigate and prosecute cases of alleged non-citizen voting. But the fact is, voter fraud in general, including voting by non-citizens, remains exceedingly rare. Case in point, as Blanche just announced these 10 indictments, there are over 3.9 million registered voters in the state of Minnesota. The justice department has filed a judicial misconduct ⁠complaint against judges in Minnesota who gave interviews to the New York Times ⁠about the immigration surge there, alleging that it was unethical and partisan. In September, ⁠judges in Minnesota told the Times (paywall) that the Trump administration had ‌a “disregard for ‌court orders” and warned that its actions posed “a grave threat to the rule of law”. Two did so on the record. The judicial misconduct complaint branded the judges’ conduct “particularly egregious”. The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, called the fact that the judges spoke ‌to the media a “clear violation of their ethical duties” and criticized them for commenting on pending cases. He also asked the judges to recuse themselves from any case involving the Department of Homeland Security, ⁠alleging they had bias against the administration. It is unusual for sitting judges to comment on the record about cases, particularly ‌those in the news, Reuters notes. The complaint was signed by the second- and third-ranking officials in the Department of Justice. Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes today, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month. A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters. Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure. Traders now see a roughly 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from about a 45% chance seen before the data, according to data ‌compiled by LSEG. The Fed is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023. Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy. More on this here: New polling from Marist university shows Sherrod Brown, the Democratic nominee in the US Senate race in Ohio, leading his Republican rival, the incumbent senator John Husted, 51% to 43%. The race is considered vital for Democrats hopes of reclaiming the Senate in the upcoming midterm elections. While Brown is up by eight points – outside the margin of error – the new poll shows that 41% of respondents say their congressional vote is mainly a vote against Donald Trump. The president’s approval rating in the Buckeye state sits at 42%. A close political ally of Donald Trump has broken from the administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda and recommended it “step back” to evaluate what it could do better. “To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” Jim Justice, a Republican senator of West Virginia, told Politico. “And in this situation, with all that’s going on and all the stuff, we probably got to step back from it and say: ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,’ and then adjust to that.” Justice, who also sits on the Senate agriculture committee, made his comments after three rancher associations condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity for negatively affecting agricultural communities. But his comments also come after an ACLU of West Virginia investigation found that about three-quarters of the more than 593 arrested by ICE in the state during “Operation Country Roads” in January had no criminal record. “Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years, and I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” Justice told Politico. Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda is a signature policy of his administration. Many voters indicated they wanted stricter immigration policies, but the intense tactics of federal agents have sparked anger nationwide. For ranchers in rural communities, ICE operations have had “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers” who assist in beef production and the cattle supply chain, the Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association said in a statement released last week. Dairy farmers have also recently raised concerns that ICE operations in rural areas could soon hurt their industries. On Capitol Hill today, we’ll be keeping an eye on the Senate’s final week in Washington before they leave for the midterm recess. Top of lawmakers’ agenda today is legislation that would allow states and utilities to consider standards to ensure tech companies foot the bill for the additional energy costs associated with power-intensive datacenters throughout the US. The bill, known as the Ratepayer Protection act, is seen as political cover for senators running in battlegrounds in the upcoming midterm cycle, where datacenter construction is a huge concern for voters. Introduced by Republican Senator John Husted, who is facing a bitter election in Ohio against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, and seen his support for datacenters become a defining issue in the race. Earlier this month, the bill passed with overwhelming support in the House, but it’s not expected to clear the upper chamber. Many Senate Democrats say the legislation is toothless, and doesn’t do enough to actually hold companies building datacenters responsible for the rise in electricity bills for local communities. Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat, called the bill a “fig leaf”, while Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, called it a “fraud” and pointed to the fact it’s entirely optional. “Instead of trying to score cheap political points with hollow proposals, Senate Republicans need to work with us to take meaningful action that will actually contain these existential risks,” Schumer said this week on the Senate floor. Following the news that the supreme court has ruled in the Trump administration’s favor, and allowed deportations to so called “third-countries” to continue, Burundi has agreed to join a group of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries who have been deported from the US. Officials in Bujumbura, Burundi’s economic capital, said they would only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links. There are no details yet on the number of deportees Burundi will take or the financial deal the country has struck with the US. The Trump administration has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely. The Guardian has previously reported on the murky deals Washington has struck with various countries to send deportees. Rachel Leingang and Riley Messer Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project. The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “summit” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet. A KFF poll from May 2026 reveals that some Maha themes resonate with a broad segment of US adults. About four in 10 say they support the Maha movement, while a majority of the public say there is not enough regulation of pesticides used in agriculture (64%) or of chemical food additives (75%). Cross-partisan support in Washington on some of these issues poses a threat to the food industry’s bottom line – though the Trump administration has largely stopped short of enacting new regulations. But several large corporations are fighting back. An effort by the Center for Food Integrity, an industry-funded non-profit, tracks public sentiment around key issues central to Maha and suggests ways that agricultural interests can counter those narratives by appealing to emotion or scientific reasoning. They call it Gaha: Growing a Healthier America.
